web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the 22-Tonne Cabin — Cargo Verticals, Charters & Real Shipments
question: What exactly flies inside Afcom's Boeing 737-800BCFs, how does the scheduled-versus-charter mix work, and what does a real shipment look like end-to-end?

epigraph.quote: Freighters do not sell seats; they sell cubic volume, payload weight, and the certainty that a factory line will not stop tomorrow morning.
epigraph.author: Air Cargo Operations Primer

web_blocks.html: Afcom Holdings runs a pure airport-to-airport air cargo model [1, 2]. It does not run delivery vans, retail parcel hubs, or door-to-door lockers [1, 2]. Instead, it sells main-deck pallet space—up to ~22 tonnes per Boeing 737-800BCF flight—to freight forwarders, integrators, and charter buyers [4, 9]. In FY26, Afcom flew 1,923 trips and moved 24,353 tonnes of freight [9]. Its domestic hubs include Chennai, Bengaluru, Delhi, and Navi Mumbai [5, 6]. Its overseas routes reach Bangkok, Hanoi, Singapore, Jakarta, Brunei, Colombo, Malé, and Dubai [5, 6, 9].

Afcom's revenue model splits into two parts: **booking mode** and **cargo vertical** [4, 5]. Booking modes cover Scheduled Network loops and On-Demand Charters [4, 5]. Cargo verticals include General/Express, Flying Pharma, Flying Fresh, and Dangerous Goods [4, 5]. In FY26, charters made up over 58% of all trips (more than 1,115 of 1,923 flights) [9]. That mix lets Afcom move planes quickly onto high-rate spot lanes instead of flying half-empty scheduled routes [9]. Scheduled flights still anchor base loads on core India–ASEAN lanes like Chennai–Bangkok and Chennai–Hanoi [5, 6]. Both modes use standard Unit Load Devices (ULDs) loaded through the 737-800BCF's hydraulic side cargo door.

web_blocks.takeaway: Afcom's 40% EBITDA margin in FY26 reflects a deliberate tilt toward >58% charter flights and passenger-belly-restricted cargo (DG, oversized, urgent pharma) rather than commoditized domestic parcels.

web_blocks.html: Investors should note one key reporting limit: Afcom does not report separate audited sales for Pharma, Fresh, DG, or Charters [1, 3]. Quarterly BSE filings group all sales under air cargo transport services [1, 3]. Still, company data shows 24,353 tonnes moved across 1,923 trips in FY26, or ~12.66 tonnes per flight [9]. On a 22-tonne B737-800BCF, that equals a ~58% weight load factor [9]. Short ferry legs and light e-commerce parcels explain the gap. Light express boxes fill the cabin volume ('cube out') before hitting the 22-tonne weight cap. Overall active network use still reached ~84% in FY26 [9].

Partner airlines extend Afcom's reach beyond its three-plane fleet [9]. Through deals with VietJet and Naero Air Corporation, Afcom issues through-airway bills from Chennai or Bengaluru into East Asia and the Pacific [9]. It hands off ULDs at hubs like Hanoi or Bangkok without flying its own planes on thin spoke routes [9]. That setup keeps flight hours focused on dense trunk lanes.

Route profits also rely on two-way load balance. Outbound flights from Chennai, Bengaluru, and Delhi carry electronics parts, auto spares, pharma, and fresh produce to Singapore, Bangkok, Hanoi, and Colombo [6, 21]. Return freight into India—such as ASEAN factory parts and express parcels—keeps round-trip use near ~84% [9, 10]. Without backhaul cargo, empty return legs quickly hurt per-flight margins [9, 10].

Afcom's airport-to-airport focus skips heavy ground-fleet spending [1, 6]. It targets urgent B2B goods like electronics, auto parts, pharma, and express parcels [6, 21]. When shippers need 24-to-48-hour delivery over ocean freight, they pay higher air rates [21]. Keeping that high-yield mix as the fleet grows from three to five narrowbodies will decide future revenue per tonne. Chennai's slot access near southern auto and electronics plants gives Afcom a natural base for overnight runs [6, 21]. Watching tonnes per trip alongside total tonnage shows whether new routes are filling up cleanly [9]. Strong two-way loads on Singapore, Bangkok, and Hanoi legs keep block-hour profits steady [6, 9, 21]. Empty return flights would quickly erode those gains when charter demand cools [9, 10].

book_paragraphs: Picture a Boeing 737-800 sitting on the cargo apron at Chennai International Airport at 1:00 AM. There are no passenger seats, no overhead bins, and no cabin crew serving coffee. Instead, the fuselage has been cut open with a massive hydraulic main-deck cargo door, and a reinforced floor with ball-mats and roller tracks is ready to swallow eleven full-size cargo pallets—roughly 22 tonnes of freight. That single image is Afcom Holdings' entire business model.

Unlike Blue Dart or FedEx, Afcom does not own a fleet of delivery vans knocking on residential doors. It operates strictly airport-to-airport. Its customers are freight forwarders, global integrators, and industrial shippers who bring cargo to the airport cargo terminal and pick it up at the destination tarmac. Within that 22-tonne tube, Afcom runs four branded verticals—General/Express cargo, Flying Pharma for temperature-sensitive medicines, Flying Fresh for perishables like seafood and produce, and Dangerous Goods for chemicals and lithium batteries that commercial passenger airlines are legally barred from carrying in their bellies.

book_callouts.title: CHARTERS VS. SCHEDULED LOOPS
book_callouts.text: In FY26, more than 58% of Afcom's 1,923 flights were charters rather than fixed-schedule runs. Charters command higher yields and eliminate empty-leg risk, but they also mean revenue is inherently more episodic than a contracted overnight parcel network.

book_subsections.title: Walking Through Real Shipments
paragraphs: To see how the economics work in practice, consider two real-world shipments. First, an automotive electronics plant outside Chennai faces an assembly-line shutdown because ocean containers from Southeast Asia are delayed by two weeks. Through an air-charter broker, the manufacturer books a full Afcom B737-800BCF charter from Chennai to Hanoi. Within hours, 18 tonnes of palletized components clear customs, roll onto the main deck, and land in Vietnam the same night. Afcom prices the entire round-trip aircraft block hours upfront, capturing high-margin charter economics with zero load-factor risk.

Now contrast that with a scheduled Flying Fresh and Dangerous Goods rotation. A Tamil Nadu seafood exporter books 10 tonnes of chilled catch bound for resort islands in Malé, while an industrial supplier books UN-certified lithium battery modules from Chennai to Bangkok—goods that IndiGo's passenger aircraft bellies cannot legally carry. Afcom's General Sales and Service Agents aggregate these smaller airway bills into full main-deck pallets, maximizing yield per cubic meter across the 24,353 tonnes it moved in FY26.

book_subsections.title: Why Tonnes Per Flight Tell Only Half the Story
paragraphs: If you divide 24,353 tonnes by 1,923 flights in FY26, you get an average of 12.66 tonnes per trip on an aircraft rated for 22 tonnes. At first glance, that looks like 58% capacity utilization—until you remember how air cargo actually loads. Lightweight e-commerce parcels and electronics packaging 'cube out' the cabin volume long before they 'weigh out' the aircraft floor.

Meanwhile, Afcom reported ~84% overall network utilization across its three freighters. Combining high-density industrial charters with volumetric express and interline transfers into partner carriers like VietJet lets Afcom keep its narrowbodies flying productive hours without chasing low-yield domestic bulk freight.

book_subsections.title: The Backhaul Imperative on ASEAN Cargo Lanes
paragraphs: Every cargo airline lives or dies by the round-trip math. Flying a 22-tonne Boeing 737-800BCF packed with Chennai automotive electronics or Tamil Nadu pharmaceuticals outbound to Singapore or Hanoi is only half the equation; if that same aircraft flies back to India half-empty, the fuel burn and crew hours of the return leg eat away the outbound profit.

That is why Afcom's network of General Sales and Service Agents across India, Hong Kong, Singapore, Thailand, Japan, South Korea, China, and Taiwan matters so much operationally. Those GSSAs aggregate return shipments—electronics sub-assemblies, specialty chemicals, and cross-border express parcels—so that Afcom's three freighters averaged roughly 12.7 tonnes per trip across 1,923 flights in FY26, sustaining an 84 percent network utilization rate.

Even so, the mix still skews toward charter work, which accounted for over 58 percent of FY26 trips. Charters command rich spot rates during maritime disruptions like the Red Sea crisis, but they lack the multi-year predictability of contracted scheduled block-space agreements.

book_subsections.title: Why Airport-to-Airport Beats Door-to-Door for a Small Fleet
paragraphs: Notice the deliberate simplicity of Afcom's business model: it operates strictly airport-to-airport. Unlike Blue Dart or Delhivery, Afcom does not own thousands of delivery vans, city sorting hubs, or last-mile couriers. Its customers are freight forwarders and General Sales and Service Agents who handle pickup and final delivery while relying on Afcom for reliable main-deck uplift between Chennai, Bengaluru, Delhi, and ASEAN gateways.

Keeping the model airport-to-airport avoids massive fixed ground-network overhead and explains how a relatively lean organization can post 37 to 40 percent EBITDA margins when aircraft fly at 84 percent utilization. The trade-off is that Afcom sits one step removed from the end shipper, making its pricing power dependent on freight-forwarder relationships and regional belly-capacity supply.

Keep that geographic and customer footprint in mind as we move into unit economics. When three 22-tonne Boeing 737-800BCFs fly 1,923 trips a year across Chennai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Navi Mumbai, Singapore, Bangkok, Hanoi, and Dubai, small shifts in return-leg load factors or GSSA pricing ripple straight through to the bottom line.

Every additional city pair—whether connecting Bengaluru to Bangkok or Delhi to Dubai—tests whether Afcom can replicate its Chennai hub economics without diluting load factors. Watching payload per flight alongside total tonnage carried gives us an early read on route maturity.
Understanding that airport-to-airport focus prepares us for Chapter 3, where we dissect every rupee of revenue from the tarmac down to operating cash flow and lease obligations.
